# iNterpolation and EXTrapolation with beta diversity based on Hill numbers

## Estimate coverage-based pairwise gamma, alpha, beta diversities and dissimilarities

The object Dists contains pairwise diversity/dissimilarity matrices for each of $q = 0, 1$, and $2$. Diversity metrics are standardized as follows: gamma diversity represents the effective number of species in the entire assemblage; alpha diversity reflects the mean joint diversity or the effective number of species-assemblage combinations per actual assemblage; and beta diversity quantifies the effective number of assemblages based on (unweighted) species raw abundance datasets, ranging from 1 to N, where $beta = 1$ indicates identical species raw abundance datasets across assemblages, and $beta = N$ indicates no shared species among assemblages.  

Additional standardized dissimilarity and turnover indices include $1-C$, the standardized Sørensen-type non-overlap index, which measures the average proportion of non-shared species in an assemblage and corresponds to Sørensen, Horn, and Morisita-Horn dissimilarities for $q = 0, 1$, and $2$ , respectively. $1-U$, the standardized Jaccard-type non-overlap index, represents the proportion of non-shared species in the pooled assemblage. $1-V$, the standardized Sørensen-type turnover index, captures species turnover relative to alpha diversity, while $1-S$, the standardized Jaccard-type turnover index, measures species turnover relative to gamma diversity.  For more details, see [Chao et al. (2023)](https://doi.org/10.1002/ecm.1588), [Chao et al. (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13233), [Chiu et al. (2014)](https://doi.org/10.1890/12-0960.1), and [Chao et al. (2016)](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-22461-9_8).

```{r}
# Generate list of all sample combination pairs 
# species abundance matrix with sample as columns and species as rows
sp <- t(spp[!zero,])
N=ncol(sp) # number of sample
p <- combn(N, 2)
dl <- NULL
for(i in 1:dim(p)[2]) dl[[i]] <- sp[, p[,i]]
# Empty matrix to fill the pariwise dissimilarity later
m <- matrix(0, ncol=N, nrow=N) %>% as.data.frame
row.names(m) <- colnames(sp)
names(m) <- colnames(sp)
```

```{r, eval=FALSE}
library(foreach)
library(doSNOW) 

# Function for iNterpolation and EXTrapolation of gamma, beta, alpha, 1-C, 1-U, 1-V, 1-S based on Hill number 
iNEXT.beta3D_fun <- function(x, ...){
  iNEXTbeta3D(x, q = c(0, 1, 2), ...) %>% lapply(FUN = function(x) lapply(x, FUN = function(x) x[5]))
}  

# We set the sample coverage = 0.7, which is the same as the alpha diversity analysis
cl<-makeCluster(16) # change the 16 to your number of CPU cores
registerDoSNOW(cl) # register the SNOW parallel backend with the foreach package
est <- foreach(i=1:length(dl), .packages=c("iNEXT.beta3D", "dplyr")) %dopar% iNEXT.beta3D_fun(dl[[i]], level=0.9, nboot=100)
stopCluster(cl) # stop a SNOW cluster

save(est, file="../Rdata/Dists.rda")
```

# Sorensen-type non-overlap dissimilarity (1-C) 
* q = 0 for Sørensen dissimilarity
* q = 1 for Horn dissimilarity
* q = 2 for Morisita-Horn dissimilarity
* Dissimilarities are standardized by 70% sample coverage (same as alpha diversity analysis)

```{r}
load("../Rdata/Dists.rda")
# Extract 1-C dissimilarity for q = 0, 1, 2
q0 <- lapply(est, FUN=function(x)x[[1]][["1-C"]][[1]][[1]]) %>% unlist
q1 <- lapply(est, FUN=function(x)x[[1]][["1-C"]][[1]][[2]]) %>% unlist
q2 <- lapply(est, FUN=function(x)x[[1]][["1-C"]][[1]][[3]]) %>% unlist

# Many with negative dissimilarities
q0[order(q0)][1:100]

# Set negative dissimilarities to zero
# Anne Chao's suggestion
q0[q0<0] <- 0
q1[q1<0] <- 0
q2[q2<0] <- 0

d <- list(q0, q1, q2)
names(d) <- 0:2

sor1 <- lapply(d, FUN = function(x){
  for(i in 1:dim(p)[2]){
  c1 <- p[1, i]
  c2 <- p[2, i]
  m[c2, c1] <- x[i]
  }
  as.dist(m)
})
```

# Nonmetric Multidimensional Scaling (nMDS)

```{r}
mds <- lapply(sor1, FUN=function(x){
  out <- metaMDS(x)
  out$fit_concentration <- envfit(out, div[!zero ,c("SST", "TOC", "TN", "TP", "TIC", "Dino")] %>% scale)
  return(out)
})

# Combine mds object with alpha diversity data
mds[[1]]$div <- cbind(div[!zero, 1:28], qD = div$d0[!zero])
mds[[2]]$div <- cbind(div[!zero, 1:28], qD = div$d1[!zero], qE = div$e1[!zero])
mds[[3]]$div <- cbind(div[!zero, 1:28], qD = div$d2[!zero], qE = div$e2[!zero])

mds[[1]]$qD.lab <- expression(""^0*italic(D))
mds[[2]]$qD.lab <- expression(""^1*italic(D))
mds[[3]]$qD.lab <- expression(""^2*italic(D))

mds[[1]]$panel.lab <- "(a)"
mds[[2]]$panel.lab <- "(b)"
mds[[3]]$panel.lab <- "(c)"
```

# Distance-based redundent analysis (dbRDA)

```{r}
db <- lapply(sor1, FUN=function(x){
  out <- capscale(x ~ SST + TOC + TN + TP + TIC + Dino, data = div[!zero ,c("SST", "TOC", "TN", "TP", "TIC", "Dino")])
  fit <- as.data.frame(out$CCA$biplot)
  sc <- min(abs(c(range(out$CCA$u[,1]), range(out$CCA$u[,1]))))
  fit <- fit*sc
  fit$label <- row.names(fit)
  out$fit <- fit
  return(out)
})

# Combine mds object with alpha diversity data
db[[1]]$div <- cbind(div[!zero, 1:28], qD = div$d0[!zero])
db[[2]]$div <- cbind(div[!zero, 1:28], qD = div$d1[!zero], qE = div$e1[!zero])
db[[3]]$div <- cbind(div[!zero, 1:28], qD = div$d2[!zero], qE = div$e2[!zero])

db[[1]]$qD.lab <- expression(""^0*italic(D))
db[[2]]$qD.lab <- expression(""^1*italic(D))
db[[3]]$qD.lab <- expression(""^2*italic(D))

db[[1]]$panel.lab <- "(a)"
db[[2]]$panel.lab <- "(b)"
db[[3]]$panel.lab <- "(c)"
```

```{r, fig.width=8, fig.height=16}
lapply(db, FUN=function(x){
  dat <- cbind(x$CCA$u, x$div)
  lab <- data.frame(x$fit[,1:2]*2) # Environmental vectors
  lab$label <- row.names(lab)
  out <- summary(x)
  d1f <- round(out$cont$importance[2, 1]*100,1) # RDA1 variance explained of the fit
  d1t <- round(out$cont$importance[2, 1]*100*out$constr.chi/out$tot.chi, 1) # RDA1 variance explained of the total
  d2f <- round(out$cont$importance[2, 2]*100,1) # # RDA2 variance explained of the fit
  d2t <- round(out$cont$importance[2, 2]*100*out$constr.chi/out$tot.chi, 1) # # RDA1 variance explained of the total
ggplot()+
    geom_point(data=dat, aes(x=CAP1, y=CAP2, fill=Period2, size = qD), pch=21, alpha = 0.8)+
    stat_ellipse(data=dat, aes(x=CAP1, y=CAP2, linetype = Period2, colour=Period2), type="t")+
    geom_segment(data=lab, aes(x=0, y=0, xend=CAP1, yend=CAP2), size=1, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2,"cm")), colour=alpha("red", 0.5))+
    geom_label_repel(data=lab, aes(x=CAP1, y=CAP2, label=label), colour="gray10", fill=alpha("white", 0.7), size=5, label.padding = unit(0.2, "lines"))+
    scale_fill_viridis_d(direction = -1)+
    scale_colour_viridis_d(direction = -1)+
    guides(fill = guide_legend(order=1), size = guide_legend(order=3), linetype = guide_legend(order=1), colour = guide_legend(order=1))+
    labs(x=bquote("dbRDA1"~(.(d1f)*"% of fit and"~.(d1t)*"% of total")), 
         y=bquote("dbRDA1"~(.(d2f)*"% of fit and"~.(d2t)*"% of total")), 
         fill="Period", size=x$qD.lab, linetype="Period", colour="Period", title = x$panel.lab)+  
    theme_bw() %+replace% large
}) %>% wrap_plots(ncol=1)
```

# Indicator Species Analysis (ISA)

The Indicator Value (IndVal), as defined by [Dufrêne & Legendre (1997)](https://doi.org/10.1890/0012-9615(1997)067[0345:SAAIST]2.0.CO;2), represents a measure of species specificity and fidelity within a specified group, such as pre-MPT, MPT, post-MPT. Specifically, IndVal is calculated as square root of the product of relative abundance (i.e., specificity) and relative frequency (i.e., fidelity) of a species present in the defined group. The specificity measures how exclusive a species to a particular group and is equal to the mean species abundance in target group divided by the sum of mean species abundances across all groups. On the other hand, fidelity measures how often a species occurs within a group and is equal to the number of sites within the target group where species is present divided by the total number of sites in the target group.

The Indicator Value (IndVal) takes a value of 0 when a species is absent from the group and reaches a maximum of 1 when the species is found in all sites of only that group and not in any others. Therefore, the highest IndVal values are indicative of species that are abundant in one group but completely absent in others, while uncommon species typically yield low IndVal values due to their low fidelity. Conversely, species that are widespread across all groups will show high fidelity and thus high IndVal scores. The statistical significance of these IndVal values is assessed through a permutation test, which is performed 999 times. 

The statistical significance of these IndVal values (or species-group associations) can be assessed through a permutation test (999 times) on the null hypothesis that the IndVal values in a specific group (or combination of groups) is not higher than the other groups.

## Indicator species in each region

A total of 37 out of 51 species were identified as significant indicator species in the Pre, MPT, Post, and MPT+Post periods. Pre+MPT+Post period do not have p values, because no permutation test is conducted for species in the group encompassing all three periods. 

```{r}
library(indicspecies)
# Indicator species
  IndVal <- multipatt(spp, sam$Period2, permutations=999)
  # Convert output to long format
  long <- cbind(Species=row.names(IndVal$A) %>% rep(each = 7),
                   # Specificity (= relative abundance)
                  pivot_longer(IndVal$A %>% as.data.frame, col=everything(), names_to = "index", values_to = "specificity"),
                  # Fidelity (= frequency of occurrence)
                  pivot_longer(IndVal$B %>% as.data.frame, col=everything(), names_to = "index", values_to = "fidelity")[,2],
                  # Indicator value (square root of A * B)
                  pivot_longer(IndVal$str %>% as.data.frame, col=everything(), names_to = "index", values_to = "stat")[,2]
                  )
# Add p values to the max indicator values among group (only those are consider indicator and tested)
long$p.value <- NA
long$index <- factor(long$index, levels=c("Pre", "MPT", "Post", "Pre+MPT", "MPT+Post", "Pre+Post", "Pre+MPT+Post"))
S <- IndVal$sign
S$index <- factor(S$index, levels=1:7, labels=c("Pre", "MPT", "Post", "Pre+MPT", "MPT+Post", "Pre+Post", "Pre+MPT+Post"))
keep <- match(paste(row.names(S), S$index), paste(long$Species, long$index))
long$p.value[keep] <- S$p.value
long <- lapply(group_split(long, index), FUN=function(x)x[order(-x$p.value, x$stat, decreasing = TRUE),]) %>% ldply
# Indicator species with p value 
wp <- subset(long, stat!=0 & !is.na(p.value))
# Indicator species without p value
np <- subset(long, index == "Pre+MPT+Post" & is.na(p.value))
np <- subset(np, !np$Species %in% wp$Species)

# Combine significant and non-significant indicator species
all_species <- rbind(wp, np)
all_species$Group <- as.character(all_species$index)
all_species$Group[all_species$p.value >=0.05 | is.na(all_species$p.value)] <- "N.S."
all_species$Group <- factor(all_species$Group, levels = c("Pre", "MPT", "Post", "MPT+Post", "N.S."))
all_species$Label <- sub(" ", "~~", paste("italic(", sub(" *\\(.*| *\\var. egregius.*", "", all_species$Species), ")", sep="")) 

ord <- order(all_species$Group, -all_species$stat)
all_species <- all_species[ord,]
all_species[,-8] %>% kable(caption = "Indicator species") %>% kable_classic()

# Top 3 indicator species from each group
top_species <- all_species %>% group_split(Group) %>% lapply(FUN=function(x)x[order(-x$stat),][1:3,]) %>% ldply %>% subset(!is.na(stat))
top_species[,-8] %>% kable(caption = "Only show the top three significant indicator species from each group. The Post period only have two significant indicator species. Three species with the highsest indicator values from Pre+MPT+Post are included. However, they are not significant indicator sepcies, because no permutation test was conducted") %>% kable_classic()
```

## Cluster Analysis

Ward's minimum variance method was applied to Sørensen dissimilarities (q = 0), Horn dissimilarities (q = 1), and Morisita-Horn dissimilarities (q = 2) among the samples. This method was also utilized for Hellinger distances between species. The heatmap illustrates the species count after applying a fourth root transformation. Due to the large number of columns representing species, the figures for the full species list are not shown. Heatmaps will be shown based on indicator species later.

```{r}
library(pheatmap)
library(RColorBrewer)

pheatmap2 <- function(mat, x, ...){
  
  # Hellinger distances between species
  dcols <- decostand(mat, "hellinger") %>% as.matrix %>%t %>% dist
  
  hc <- hclust(x, method="ward.D2")
  clust <- cutree(hc, k=4)
  
  # rearrange by latitude
  nc <- aggregate(sam$Age_ka[!zero], by=list(clust), FUN=max)[,2] %>% order(decreasing = TRUE)
  clust <- factor(clust, nc, 1:4)
  
  annotation_row <- data.frame(Period=sam$Period2[!zero], Cluster=clust)
  rownames(annotation_row) <- sam$Age_ka[!zero]
  annotation_colors <- list(
    Period = c("Pre"="#f3c300", "MPT"="#875692", "Post"="#f38400"),
    Cluster = c("1"="#a1caf1", "2"="#be0032", "3"="#c2b280", "4"="#848482"))
    
  pheatmap(mat^0.25, 
         color = brewer.pal(9, "Blues"), 
         clustering_distance_rows = x, 
         clustering_distance_cols = dcols, 
         clustering_method = "ward.D2", 
         legend_breaks = 0:3,
         legend_labels = (0:3)^4,
         cutree_rows = 4, 
         annotation_row = annotation_row, 
         annotation_colors = annotation_colors,
         , ...)
}
```

### Heatmap base on idicator species and Sørensen dissimilarities (q = 0) 

```{r, fig.width=12, fig.height=12}
pheatmap2(spp[!zero, top_species$Species], sor1[[1]], fontsize_col=12, show_rownames=FALSE, angle_col=45)
```
